This study develops novel conversational Lyapunov theorems that establish an equivalence between the asymptotic stability of a non-linear regulation system and the boundedness of its trajectories, even in scenarios involving unbounded controls. Distinguishing ourselves from prior work, we allow control functions to depend on both the system's state and time explicitly, and we accommodate controls that are continuous only with respect to state variables, while maintaining measurability in time. We further address cases where controls exhibit continuity along specific directions, a flexibility necessitated by applications in adaptive control where control laws possess singularities on subsets of the state manifold. These advancements are demonstrated through their application to determining global stability in non-linerlyly stable systems with parameterized feedback and bounded controllers.

This study introduces a deep learning framework utilizing a generative adversarial network (GAN) to reconstruct turbulent velocity fields from undersampled measured data. The model is trained on datasets generated by direct numerical simulation (DNS) covering a spectrum of Reynolds numbers, enabling it to accurately recover velocity fields at Reynolds numbers present in the training data as well as generalize to Reynolds numbers not included during training. Trained effectively on high-Reynolds number turbulent flows, the system produces results with significantly higher fidelity than conventional linear reconstruction methods, such as zero- or sinc-based interpolation. Furthermore, when compared to recent approaches like those by Li et al. (2019), this method yields superior accuracy and demonstrates the additional capability to estimate turbulent structure functions.

This review examines debates surrounding solutions to initial value problems where either part or all components of the wave function start as non-negative real values, with future states constrained by linear or nonlinear variants of the Schr\"odinger, Klein-Gordon, or Wick-rotated equations. I argue that standard claims regarding unitary evolution preserving such special characteristics are frequently incorrect, despite the widespread application of these properties in arguments for quantum objective realities. Furthermore, I suggest that interactions with environment-induced decoherence often fail to account solely for the loss of quantum coherence when restricted to these specific initial value subsets.

Uncertainty modeling remains a critical challenge in deep learning assurance, yet most current methods operate in constrained lab environments and fail to reflect real-world conditions. This discrepancy arises because modern models generalize poorly to the full spectrum of natural image distributions. To address this, we introduce a novel distribution-matching framework that leverages an estimated energy distribution over the natural image space to reinforce uncertainty outputs. By training uncertainty estimators to align with this robust natural scene distribution, we enhance their validity outside controlled settings. In addition, we develop an automatic, self-calibrating training protocol that requires no manual tuning or labeled data. Experiments across multiple architectures and uncertainty methodologies demonstrate significant improvements over prior approaches.

Although significant progress has been made in applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) across diverse tasks, exploring the field's overall advancement and pinpointing specific obstacles remains challenging. We address this gap by introducing **L2Explorer**, a specialized RL evaluation platform designed to facilitate continuous assessment and identify key barriers. Drawing heavily on the **LifeLong** structure, L2Explorer hosts a unified collection of benchmark suites that enable a standardized, holistic, and consistent approach to RL testing. We propose a rigorous framework to evaluate and recognize various RL algorithms within this setting. Initial experiments reveal that **P3 off-policy methods** and **on-policy methods** achieve comparable performance across most suites, whereas **P3 on-policy strategies** dominate in others, specifically **LIFLB** and **OBVL**. Furthermore, we observe that **P3 on-policy methods** maintain performance consistency across suite versions, a trait not shared by off-policy approaches which suffer degradation as suites evolve. Finally, we recognize **LIFLB** as a promising emerging direction within RL research. All accompanying code and resources can be accessed at https://github.com/zhongong/L2Explorer.

We have developed a monitoring framework designed to track declarative processes executing ECPL rules, a format known for its use in business rule management systems. By leveraging event streams, this framework enables the straightforward expression of monitoring concerns through continuous queries. Consequently, such queries remain easily adaptable and can be maintained separately from the business logic itself. These continuous queries dynamically generate traces that reflect the system's behavior, automatically identify when a trace fulfills specific monitoring constraints, and trigger the corresponding actions. Within our approach, these query results are categorized into two distinct functions: a monitoring function responsible for identifying alert conditions, and a search function for locating data that satisfies these constraints. The realization of the monitoring function within these declarative rule processes facilitates automatic notification and alerting mechanisms. Meanwhile, the implementation of the search function supports ad-hoc analysis and inductive analysis, such as applying logical deduction to discover new rules based on observed data patterns.

One-dimensional optical quasicrystals consist of periodic layers whose thicknesses follow a simple linear inhomogeneous recurrence relation, producing a forbidden gap within the photonic band structure. When certain layer pairs swap positions, leading to two possible coupling patterns, we find that these patterns generate distinct, wide localization regions where no states exist even outside the primary band gap. As the linear recurrence relation transitions from a expanding to a contracting regime across the gap, strong coupling between adjacent pairs causes optical states to shift and split into two separate, narrow bands situated inside the gap. We term this phenomenon reentrant delocalization shifting. Additionally, we experimentally construct a 31-periodic sequence of layers, demonstrating a transition of optical shift and observing reentrant shifting behavior that mirrors the theoretical predictions. Finally, we propose a model using coupled oscillators to analyze the system's mechanical response, suggesting feasible methods to engineer and detect similar effects in other physical contexts.

Liger, a new near-infrared (NIR) imager and spectrometer recently installed at the W. M. Keck Observatory, was developed as a collaborative project by the National Astronomical Observatories of China (NAOC) and the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute (KASI). This system capitalizes on the superior capabilities of the Keck telescopes, supporting a broad spectrum of research across various fields. This paper details the architecture, design principles, and implementation of the Liger data processing system, along with the software interfaces required for exposure control, guiding, and reduction workflows within the MIDAS environment. Additionally, we outline the specific software modules essential for operational control and scientific analysis using Python programming language. Finally, this article describes the integration of NAOC's modeling software, MOMENT, which utilizes Python code to process and deconvolve the data obtained from the Liger system.

Spatial mode demultiplexing (SMD) of single photons in linear optical quantum computing (LOQC) acts both as a fundamental component and a crucial benchmark for assessing the progress of scaling efforts in this field. Currently, large nonlinearities required for deterministic two-photon spatial switch operations conflict with the need for highly scalable architectures. This study proposes an alternative approach utilizing bilinear interactions mediated by bi-photon nonlinear nonlinearities to achieve high-fidelity quantum state transfer (QST) between optical modes. This method relies on linearly interacting photons within cavities containing nonlinear media, utilizing a paraxial (bi-photon) interaction to achieve high-fidelity quantum state transfer (QST) between spatial modes. The proposed technique achieves a fidelity of approximately 0.999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999

This expository note outlines the classification of possible compactifications for smooth projective surfaces and establishes a framework for examining the intersection between the moduli space of such surfaces and its boundary within a newly introduced compactification. Current large language models (LLMs) are typically deployed with a fixed set of capabilities, which creates significant constraints when addressing specialized domains. We introduce a class of nonlocal diffusion models featuring instantaneous nonlinear interactions, formulated to match the accuracy of their corresponding local counterparts while converging to fractional diffusion under appropriate limits. During photography, images are frequently captured while moving, particularly through vigorous or unintentional motion like shaking. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel two-fluid large-eddy simulation framework featuring advanced subgrid-scale closures designed specifically for Rayleigh-B\'enard convection. We demonstrate that this approach successfully reproduces the characteristics of boundary layers and the energy and flux spectra observed in direct numerical simulations.

The research establishes that there exists a specific threshold, termed the "frog number," which delineates a bifurcation: below this value, the limit covers only a vanishingly small fraction of the tree, whereas above it, the limit encompasses every reachable node. Furthermore, the article derives a connection between this number and the essential density required for other processes—such as Ligh's interactive system—to fail convergence. Crucially, the work proves this limit equals the limit in cases where an upstream ancestor exists for a substantial cohort of root-generated frogs, effectively identifying the limit as both the measure of permanent impact and a measure of initial population breadth.

Security researchers have developed Decision-Based Black-Box (DBBB) attacks to evaluate the robustness of machine learning (ML) systems by exploiting gradient leaks via adversarial examples. Results demonstrate that the WDBBA approach achieves a significant improvement in both efficiency and performance compared to other existing solutions.

Given a graph $G$ and a subset $S \subseteq V(G)$, the geodetic distance $d_G(S)$ represents the length of all shortest graphs connecting any two vertices in $S$. This paper proves that the strong geodetic recognition problem is $NP$-hard for general graphs and presents several related findings.

We examine the setting of online path learning, where a system non-adaptively supplies a suboptimal policy yielding suboptimal experiences in a Markov decision process (MDP), in contrast to prior online path learning research that assumed access to an optimal policy yielding optimal experiences. Our analysis introduces two new lower bounds: one establishing that a substantially greater number of exploration steps is required when limited to suboptimal experiences, and another indicating that substantially more exploration iterations are necessary if only a bounded count of suboptimal experiences can be received. Based on these bounds, we present an exploration-heavy algorithm that matches the near-optimal performance of methods used under optimal experience conditions for the scenario of full access to suboptimal experiences.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has recently enabled training robust visual representation by eliminating the need for extensive labeled data. However, incorporating annotated datasets remains essential for ensuring robustness and ensuring controlled annotation, which can be resource-intensive and time-consuming. To mitigate this burden, we introduce a method that trains models using only unlabeled data by removing expert demonstration from the pipeline. Our approach, Co-Observation Learning (COOL), adapts contrastive learning to a single-stream framework. It generates positive and negative sample pairs through data augmentation and the aggregation of embedded knowledge. Specifically, we employ aggregation to construct a bank of enhanced prototypes from standard augmented images. These prototype embeddings then serve as anchors for a contrastive loss function applied to their corresponding augmented variants. We further refine this loss function by assigning adaptive weighting based on the variability within the prototype embeddings. Demonstrated on several standard benchmarks, COOL achieves state-of-the-art performance using purely unlabeled training data.

Additionally, this work establishes a direct formula for computing the PAC code of an $n$-bit integer, far surpassing the complexity of current metric code calculations, and successfully proves the convergence of the dimension formula for these codes. Numerical simulations and real-world tests validate both the code's efficacy and the accuracy of this derived metric formula in practical scenarios, and finally, the paper presents a generalized degree-$d$ extension, named $d$-PAC code, and its corresponding metric for inputs in natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$.

We analyzed tidal structures around 150 early-type galaxies (ETGs) with effective radii $>10$ kpc using HSC-SSP imaging data. The formation of solid bodies in protoplanetary disks faces a significant hurdle: the gravitational focusing required for planetesimals to form is too slow given the disk's limited lifetime. Current theories suggest that the growth of planetesimals into massive, rapidly growing planetary embryos is driven by the formation of long-lived, dense clusters known as self-sustaining whirls within the disk. In our study, we utilized the Fokkebaard-Amsden (FAB) code to simulate the behavior of these whirls. We first established baseline models using standard, non-ideal gas laws and then systematically altered key parameters to assess their impact. Additionally, we incorporated a model for dry friction between moving solid bodies to evaluate growth rates. Our modified FAB simulations revealed that the death of these whirls is often dictated by the dissipation of excess energy and vorticity, which can be significantly altered by deviations from ideal gas conditions. Specifically, the adoption of a Van der Waals equation of state resulted in the emergence of long-lasting, dense clusters. Finally, with the inclusion of frictional damping, our models demonstrated rapid growth rates consistent with those required for planetesimal formation.

Quantum Hall states are renowned for their resilience, a trait largely stemming from long-lived neutral excitations that can safely traverse multiple charged quantum states. Consequently, this phenomenon allows for the conversion of neutral plasmon currents into charged currents. Furthermore, the observed dc current exhibits a magnitude proportional to the square of the neutral plason amplitude. Practically, this effect facilitates the measurement of upstream neutral plasons in QAH systems that are otherwise difficult to detect due to the absence of downstream plasmons in such quantum anomalous Hall edge channels.

Although tight-binding models are frequently employed to simulate light-matter interactions in periodic systems, the underlying quantum of nuclear positions typically breaks continuous translational symmetry. Results indicate that these newly generated symmetry-preserving models are exceptionally accurate in predicting polarizability tensors and other linear and nonlinear optical characteristics when benchmarked against time-dependent approaches based on full density functional theory. Conventional point cloud models, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), often induce information loss during point sampling or through the aggregation of cloud structures. To mitigate this, we introduce the Task-Priority (TPC) learning framework, which restructures points based on their significance to the specific task. This approach replaces standard implicit smoothness assumptions with a task-dependent one, enhancing the stability of optimized point positions and semantic predictions. A primary contribution is the introduction of Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TURB), a novel regularizer that enforces consistent semantic neighbors across multiple geometrically similar but semantically distinct points generated by various sampling methods. This regularizer transforms learning into a two-stage process: an initial optimization of smoothness assumptions using point importance weights, followed by an iterative refinement where points adjust based on task-prioritized semantic consistency. Experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves both recognition accuracy and robustness compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

To validate slotted ALOHA and CSMA performance under various scenarios, extensive simulations were conducted comparing these methods against a traditional sequential approach. Results demonstrate that both the slotted ALOHA and CSMA methods achieve mean communication latency improvements of 30% and 130%, respectively, compared to the sequential strategy.

Observing animal behavior in video footage is essential for biological research, yet conducting these analyses manually is both time-consuming and labor-intensive. Consequently, there is a critical need for the field of biology to adopt efficient computational tools for automatic behavior detection. This study introduces a straightforward, accessible, and reliable method for identifying movement in video data by leveraging open-source, "off-the-shelf" software.

We introduce an innovation to the class of Elevated-Order methods, creating a new approach known as Successive-Order Techniques (SOT). This method generates solutions to linear systems $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ by successively employing polynomials of increasingly higher degrees, ultimately yielding an $O(N^{-3})$ rate of convergence. A key advantage of SOT is its compatibility with iterative refinement; specifically, once refinement is applied, it achieves a convergence rate comparable to, or even exceeding that of, the proposed SOT itself. These attributes make the iterative SOT method an attractive candidate for solving sparse linear systems on GPU architectures. The paper also presents comprehensive numerical experiments comparing the efficiency of the traditional Schur complement method, EOT, and the iterative SOT method (both with and without iterative refinement) across three specific sparse matrix types: the mass matrix from a 3D finite element simulation, a matrix derived from a sparse LU decomposition of a banded matrix, and the adjacency matrix corresponding to a 3D torus.

We illustrate these principles first using simple model systems and subsequently by analyzing numerically non-trityronous transit data regarding the Fradkin-Jaffé potential.

We examine one-loop generation of the Higgs boson mass within the framework of the supersymmetric two-Higgs-doublet model, utilizing an intrinsically motivated potential where potential parameters are constrained by the physical masses of the top quark and NMS scalar, as well as the heavy Higgs mass. Network autoregressive (NAR) models are increasingly utilized to analyze the structural interdependencies among connected entities. This study introduces a novel linearity test designed to differentiate linear NAR models from their nonlinear counterparts, specifically those based on threshold mechanisms. Our proposed test relies on residual sums of squares (RSS) and leverages results from recent work regarding eigenvalue distributions of sparse, symmetric, and Bernoulli matrices. A proposed bootstrap methodology generates critical values for the test statistic, effectively addressing limitations in current literature concerning the derivation of limiting distributions under model sparsity and the potential for non-standard limiting behavior. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations validate the test procedure, and an empirical application examines linear versus nonlinear dynamics of U.S. state-level tourism flows.

The dynamic movement of cells and their ability to direct protein movement within membranes are fundamental to numerous biological processes. To advance understanding of these phenomena, we need modeling approaches that capture the non-linear interactions between an organism's motion and its external environment, as well as internal mechanisms. Although current models exist for both external flow and intracellular protein dynamics, a specific framework addressing mobile external agents with a distinct, physically motivated mobility is currently missing. In this study, we introduce a new model based on an effective, phenomenological friction coefficient. This coefficient accounts for the movement of red blood cells through varying fluids and the drift of membrane proteins. We demonstrate the application of this framework by deriving a general equation for the slow motion of a single protein and extending it to calculate the trajectory of an entire cell moving through a viscous fluid.

The rapid expansion of the global financial sector has coincided with a surge in illicit activities, prompting the development of various detection methodologies. Among the emerging tools is the public blockchain, which provides transparent, verifiable, and immutable ledgers for all ledger entries, enabling the retrospective tracing of fund movements. This study examines the integration of machine learning techniques and graph-based analytics to analyze complex financial trajectories of dubious actions within cryptocurrency blockchains, utilizing the Monero protocol for examination. Employing data from the FIAT currency exchange platform within the Monero-based blockchain, machine learning models were trained to pinpoint 'dubious' transactions. The research utilized a dataset comprising 1,000 'suspect' transactions and 1,000 'non-suspect' transactions, with these actions categorized as either 'obvious' (involving theft, extortion, or robbery) or 'subtle' (involving money laundering). Through a combination of machine learning algorithms and blockchain analysis, the study successfully identified both explicit and implicit suspicious actions, demonstrating that this methodology effectively maps financial routes of dubious transactions within a blockchain environment.

Topological quantum computation (TQC) has emerged as a promising strategy for building scalable and fault-resilient quantum computers. In this framework, logical quantum gates are executed through the braiding of anyonic anyons, while errors are corrected by fusing them. A fundamental challenge in TQC is ensuring that the topological protection inherent in anyons effectively shields the computation from errors, a difficulty compounded by the extreme resilience of certain anyons to perturbations. Consequently, providing the necessary energy and conditions to create, manipulate, and annihilate these anyons represents a significant experimental hurdle. Furthermore, the operational sequences required for braiding and fusion are notoriously complex to engineer and bring to fruition. We demonstrate that reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms can effectively address these issues by autonomously discovering resilient procedures for both braiding and fusion. Using the Fibonacci anyon as a concrete example, our approach successfully determines experimentally feasible protocols for operations that are safe against errors arising from photon loss, anyion decay, or unintended interactions with other defects.

In this work, we investigate the dynamics of a quantum sensor employing the dual-cavity QED configuration to execute a symmetric quantum statistical jump metrology protocol. We evaluate how the quantum nature of these leaps influences the growth of spin entanglement as well as the precision and speed of estimating a collective magnetic field. Our numerical simulations indicate that utilizing quantum jumps enables the sensor to attain the fundamental quantum leverge limit within fewer iterations compared to scenarios where jumps are treated classically. Furthermore, we observe distinct characteristics regarding the convergence of quantum coherence and the optimal durations for estimating the field strength, depending explicitly on whether the stochastic nature of quantum jumps is incorporated into the analysis.

In this study, we examine how jets interact with the medium by analyzing direct photon-hadron distributions. Our analysis involves comparing data from Au+Au collisions to those from d+Au collisions, both run at a per-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV, covering midrapidity hadrons and varying photon rapidities across two invariant mass intervals. We observe that the medium-induced enhancement of downstream hadrons (those located behind the photon) is significantly more pronounced in Au+Au than in d+Au collisions, whereas no substantial difference in this effect is seen when hadrons and photons are separated by opposite directions. Furthermore, we detect enhanced jet fragmentation asymmetry—characterized by an increase in photon-jet invariant mass and a suppression of hadrons on the photon- opposite side—which provides insight into the energy deposition of the medium.

This paper examines how network performance inconsistencies affect an application's scalability. While network reliability is a well-established concern, understanding its effect on scaling remains less explored. We identify that network metrics, specifically latency and packet loss, trigger application behavior adaptations that can either hinder or enhance scalability. To investigate this, we conducted performance tests on a cloud-deployed multiplayer game, varying network conditions across three distinct environments: physical hardware, virtual machines, and serverless functions. Our findings indicate that the nature of performance variability—whether it stems from physical or serverless infrastructures—has a lesser impact than the condition's intensity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both latency and packet loss are critical factors, with packet loss exerting a more profound influence on scale-out capabilities than latency does.

We examine a multi-armed bandit setup where a team of $k$ agents collaborates to interact with a linear function contextual bandit agent. In this framework, context inputs are generated externally and distributed among the $k$ agents, such that no single context element is visible to any one of them in full. The goal is for the agents to learn the contextual agent's preferences sufficiently to dispense a sub-optimal outcome at most once. A crucial constraint is that context information remains unshared between the agents to preserve context privacy. The contextual agent, however, may be curious about the location of context elements within the system. We find that if the contextual agent does not request context information, the cumulative regret for the contextual agent grows logarithmically with respect to the context size $L$. Conversely, if the agent is curious about context distribution, this agent may experience a linear growth in regret relative to $L$. Our findings are further limited to a linear functional form for the contextual agent's preference regarding context privacy.

In an effort to examine how telecommuting affects Scrum project outcomes, we present a study involving six software development teams from a single company. Observing a rise in remote work among Scrum implementations, the authors aimed to investigate this link. We defined telecommuting rates using data from a survey of 161 teams from our company and identified Scrum success through item velocity within a survival analysis framework. Guided by prior literature, an initial qualitative analysis explored relevant dynamics. Subsequently, a quantitative analysis identified a negative association between the proportion of remote work and Scrum success, which was further supported by longitudinal data from 161 teams from our company. Subsequent analysis of non-successful projects revealed a higher rate of remote work. While this study is limited by its focus on a single organization, it offers a rare, comprehensive look into the complexities of distributed Scrum work.

This study focuses on the dynamics of hopping robots operating on compliant terrain supported by a single leg. We developed a bi-phasic physical model consisting of vibration-dampening contact and free-air phases to simulate gravity-driven hopping behavior under these conditions. Corresponding equations of motion were derived for both intervals, with the impact transition governed by an inelastic constraint. By solving the resulting hybrid system analytically, closed-form expressions for key metrics—including hopping amplitude, peak velocity, velocity at release, and temporal durations—were obtained to characterize the locomotion. Based on these analytical models, simulation software was created to validate the robot's behavior. Furthermore, the influence of leg stiffness, leg mass, gravity, and ground compliance on the system was investigated through numerical experiments. These simulations were extended to a heavier, one-degree-of-freedom bipedal robot to verify consistency with established theoretical results. Consequently, this work enhances the understanding of legged interaction with soft ground and provides a simplified modeling framework and baseline data essential for future enhancements.

We present the initial calculations of elastic shape factors for mesons within the light-front mapping framework. By defining these factors using the ratio of the convolution of the PDFs and RPCs of two-photon-meson couplings to their $e^+e^-$-annihilation equivalents, we establish direct parallelism with hadronic shape factors. This setup allows us to derive explicit expressions for the pion and tensor meson form factors. Furthermore, we identify the necessary conditions for the confinement of quarks and gluons within hadrons while addressing the long-standing issue regarding the non-zero mass of light hadrons.

An electrohydrodynamic fan, observable within the attached droplet, serves as an effective indicator of the transition to a turbulent regime in liquid jets containing vapor particles. This optical signature, resulting from mini-EDF forces acting upon surrounding air, facilitates stronger observations of transition dynamics in trans-critical jet conditions. Observing this phenomenon helps track the shift from the jet's potential core region to its collapsed state. The presence of the fan is attributed to surface tension gradients within the hot liquid, which trigger rolling motion and stretch droplet appendages into a fan configuration. Such surface effects are absent in ambient temperature water jets, thereby distinguishing the current visual marker. The surface elasticity responsible for the effect arises from a combination of non-equilibrium thermodynamic states and the presence of a vapor skin on the liquid surface.

Although NLP systems have advanced significantly in their ability to comprehend negation within single sentences, they remain largely ineffective at inferring negation from context and applying those inferences to other utterances. This paper introduces CoNDAQA, a newly developed corpus focused on negation and the reasoning derived from it. The dataset comprises 8,000+ utterance pairs that establish a denotation through contradictory pairings, along with 500k+ three-question queries designed to test this reasoning from a third utterance. We present baseline analyses indicating current limitations in models addressing this specific task, while also showcasing the dataset's utility for evaluating and enhancing question-formation capabilities. Finally, we present an ablation study on current state-of-the-art architectures, demonstrating a measurable decline in performance on CoNDAQA compared to other similar CO2QA and CO2QA2. These findings collectively suggest that CO2QA offers a valuable resource for training models to better grasp and generate questions based on implied negation.

Structural computation involves determining specific attributes of information networks, such as node centrality measures, network components, or influence rankings. These operations are fundamental to a wide range of applications, including online advertising, spam detection, knowledge extraction, and system resilience analysis. A critical and often overlooked aspect is the fact that even seemingly minor structures can involve massive subsets of the total network, necessitating the development of highly efficient and resource-conscious algorithms to support their execution. Currently, the computational methods for these structures are typically developed in isolation, which prevents effective knowledge reuse and hinders progress. To address this, we introduce a unified framework for information network processing that facilitates the shared implementation of related computations. By implementing common functionalities within this system, we enable the rapid deployment and experimentation of new algorithms across diverse scenarios. Our approach centers on a modular design, which allows researchers to efficiently share and test alorithms across various graph structures. Key capabilities provided by this system include a persistent graph store optimized for high concurrency, a graph execution engine capable of leveraging both multi-threading and distributed computing resources, and a comprehensive algorithm library for graph processing. Furthermore, we offer a suite of new, high-performance implementations for popular centrality metrics and component finders. Experimental results demonstrate that these structures and their corresponding algorithms achieve substantial performance improvements, utilizing significantly less memory. Specifically, these tests indicate up to an eightfold increase in throughput and a reduction in memory consumption by as much as 90% when operating in distributed environments.

The generic structure of quantum annealing involves initializing the system in the ground state of a straightforward Hamiltonian, while the target ground state emerges as the ground state of a complex Hamiltonian; this ground state is reached by slowly interpolating between the two parent Hamiltonians over a specific time span known as the quantum annealing interval (QAI). Regarding this parameter, prior research has substituted the gradual interpolation with an instantaneous switch at $t=0$, producing a non-adiabaling sudden quench. Although experimentally more viable, such a sudden quench may fail to yield high-fidelity results if the switching occurs without regard to optimal conditions. To investigate these dynamics within the context of the Ising Hamiltonian and a transverse field, we apply the path-ordered time-dependent formalism within mean-field theory to model the quench process. Our analysis reveals an optimal annealing interval that minimizes excitation populations in the system post-quench, with a corresponding optimal sudden quench value of approximately $2.5$ times the inverse of the gap between field strengths. We further demonstrate experimentally that optimal insertion of QAI during sudden quenching can reduce logical bit-flip errors in quantum error-corrected scenarios involving the annealing of D-Wave machines.

Formal verification of traces generated by flexible, non-deterministic implementations of distributed systems is crucial for maintaining system consistency. This paper introduces a novel algorithm that efficiently checks the compliance of trace segments between pairs of infix or postfix computational alignment algorithms. Unlike existing methods that rely on checking individual inflexible hashes, this approach accommodates algorithms capable of aligning subsets of a trace through multiple non-unique computational interpretations. Although applicable to various algorithms of its kind, this algorithm achieves particularly polynomial complexity when used with hashing mechanisms based on cryptographic primitives such as Merkle trees, Rabin fingerprints, or SHA-256. High-temperature superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates is frequently linked to strong electron-electron interactions, yet the precise mechanisms remain elusive. A critical aspect of these interactions is magnetic exchange ($J$), which dictates the energy gap between occupied electron states and unoccupied hole states. In this study, we determine $J$ for the relevant 3$d$ electron configuration of these systems by employing a density-functional theory (DFT)-based screening approach. This method calculates the exact non-coulombic part of the exchange interaction, while the remaining contribution is derived from the effective screening theorem. Our findings indicate that $J$ is not uniform across all nickel $d$-orbitals; specifically, it varies significantly between orbitals within the same electron configuration. This non-uniformity results in an energy splitting of approximately $0.5$ eV, a value inconsistent with previous estimates based on x-ray absorption and emission spectroscopy. Consequently, a multi-band model is required to accurately describe the physics of superconducting infinite-layer nickelates, contradicting recent proposals suggesting a single-band model is adequate.

We propose to examine the electronic transport properties of cuprate superconductors employing a generalized serial-parallel (SP) model. This framework extends the conventional Falicov-Pvarianna (HP) model, which is restricted to describing the metal-insulator transition in these materials. By incorporating a small transverse hopping amplitude, our approach retains the essential physics of the insulating transition while enabling a metal with a finite Fermi liquid. Consequently, this model allows for meaningful exploration of intermediate magnetic states and their impact on interlayer conductivity. Notably, without requiring structural d-wave symmetry, the model successfully reproduces the $1/T_c$ divergence of c-axis resistivity observed experimentally. Furthermore, it accounts for temperature-dependent resistivity across an extensive regime, including the insulating behavior at high temperatures and Fermi liquid characteristics at low temperatures. We also investigate the effects of charge density order and determine the conditions under which such phenomena enhance c-axis resistivity.

The equation of dense matter is typically constrained by the speed of sound ($c_s$), particularly when comparing non-relativistic and non-relativistic equations of matter. In this study, we examine the behavior of $c_s$ in dense matter containing compact stars and strange quarks. By employing a relativistic parton-hydrodynamic model, we explore the evolution of matter under these extreme conditions. Our results indicate that $c_s$ rises rapidly with increasing density, potentially surpassing the causal limit ($c^2$) at high densities, a behavior consistent with the presence of deconfined quark matter and strange quarks. Furthermore, we explore the implications of our model for the structure and stability of compact stars, finding that the presence of $c^2$ in the equation of matter could explain the mass-radius relation observed in neutron stars. Lastly, we discuss how our model could be tested experimentally in the future.

Given a set of currently existing labeled nodes and a specific evolutionary history depicted as an unordered tree, the goal of adverse node mapping is to construct a binary, resolved tree that minimizes the total cost of misplacing those given nodes. Pre-existing methodologies for computing this cost have been limited to scenarios where all but a minimal number of node pairings are resolved; this work introduces a novel algorithm capable of handling the broader problem on general binary trees with equal cost efficiency. Furthermore, when applied to Generalized Cost (GC) costs, these findings demonstrate that the problem transitions from NP-hard to polynomial-time solvable under those constraints.

We examine the effect of phase-space squeezing and displacement on the peak photon number capacity of the Fock space, utilizing the state of squeezed shifted number states (often referred to as number analogs of squeezed states). The analysis reveals that the maximum information capacity traversing this quantum state space is achieved when the state is maximally shifted in number and squeezed. We further establish that the optimal compass state for distribution within the Fock space corresponds to an equally optimized configuration of number squeezing and displacement. Numerical results indicate that the achieved information capacity far surpasses that of previously suggested strategies, such as the circular distribution of coherent states or the recent scheme involving clouds of optimally split and squeezed vacuum states.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) represents a promising candidate for facilitating rapid planet formation within the circumstellar disks' stable regions. Recent research indicates that dust evolution exerts a significant influence on the VSI; however, existing studies have primarily focused on the disk's midplane, neglecting the stably stratified dust structures present in the outer layers. In this work, we investigate the formation and characteristics of a volatile shear instability arising from stably stratified dust development in the outer regions of protoplanetary circumstellar disks to explore its potential effects on the formation and evolution of these disks. We find that dust evolution occurring within the disk outer layers can generate an additional form of VSI, which we term "boundary-layer VSI," situated between the dust midplane and the stratified dust surface. This boundary-layer VSI produces significant nonaxisymmetric velocity fluctuations and enhances the formation and enhancement of existing planets, potentially leading to the formation and enhancement of additional planets and increasing the overall complexity of the system.

This paper introduces a new technique termed Dynamic Entrances with Global Mean Pooling (DEGMP). It addresses a key constraint in existing methods, which rely on static entrances and fail to effectively integrate the specific, variable characteristics of diverse loss functions. Our approach leverages these dynamic entrances and implements a global mean pooling strategy to calculate the precise gradient scaling factor required for each individual loss function. Through experiments on multiple benchmarks within the self-supervised learning domain, we demonstrate that our method significantly enhances both the clustering performance and the overall quality of the generated representations compared to current state-of-the-art static entrance architectures. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analytical study of dynamic entrances and their synergy with global mean pooling to derive a new, streamlined static entrance mechanism. Experimental evidence confirms that incorporating this optimized static entrance into various leading models yields superior results.

High-precision astrometry relies on relativistic analysis, where the PPN parameter $\gamma$ significantly influences measured stellar parallaxes. This paper examines how $\gamma$ affects parallax estimates by comparing a gaia-like astrometric model under two scenarios: one where $\gamma$ is fixed at its standard value of 1, and another where it is treated as a free parameter during the fitting process. The study utilizes a gaia-inspired point source model, a white dwarf model, and a binary system model, evaluating performance through Monte Carlo simulations involving $10^6$ trials for each case. Parallax biases and their associated uncertainties were assessed for each model type, revealing that unphysical values of $\gamma$ can cause significant shifts even for fixed values. Furthermore, allowing $\gamma$ to vary freely introduces parallax uncertainties approximately 10% higher than those observed when the parameter remains fixed at its true value.

Creating reduced-order models (ROMs) is essential for managing the high computational costs associated with detailed nonlinear dynamical systems. While traditional reduction techniques rely on linearization and fail under full nonlinear conditions, advanced methods like neural network-based manifold discovery can effectively capture nonlinear dynamics, albeit with extensive training times. We introduce a new, fast model reduction framework based on iterative refinement that rapidly generates an efficient ROM using limited data. By leveraging sparse gradient descent optimization to fit differential equations directly to trajectory snapshots, our approach achieves a speedup of two orders of magnitude compared to standard techniques, requiring data only from a single simulation. Crucially, this method avoids the pitfalls associated with frequent regularization needs in scenarios with scarce dataset sizes. Validation through various nonlinear systems demonstrates that the resulting ROMs maintain exceptional accuracy and provide highly precise long-term dynamical predictions.

In the case of an unbiased estimator with minimum variance, a general formulation for minimum variance is provided. Reading and problem-solving require a solid grasp of the text's content, making reading comprehension a fundamental skill. Since reading also serves as a gateway to other subjects, enhancing it significantly boosts academic and career success. Over the last ten years, Knowledge Tracing (KT), which models a student's evolving proficiency with specific content, has emerged as a dominant technique for improving personalized education. Although KT can be implemented with various methods, advanced implementations now rely on Deep Learning (DL) to achieve state-of-the-art outcomes on standard datasets. However, current DL-based approaches often act as "black boxes," offering poor insights into why they make specific predictions, which impedes efforts to enhance or deploy them in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, there is currently no unified evaluation protocol for DL-KT models, making cross-method comparisons difficult. To address these gaps, we introduced **pyKT**, an open-source framework that unifies data, preprocessing, and deep learning knowledge tracing models. By enabling the rapid experimentation with multiple models on consistent formats, pyKT fosters broader exploration and facilitates fair benchmarking. We demonstrate the utility of pyKT by conducting a comprehensive comparative analysis of seven state-of-the-art DL-KT models using this platform.

While proof assistants like Coq and Isabelle/IsaFoL have long supported automation via plugins, integrating similar features seamlessly into VeriFiFi remains challenging. This limitation largely stems from the complexity of mapping diverse proof formats generated by modern tools to the specific, intricate structures required by each automation tool. To address this hurdle and enable greater interoperability among modern SMT-based certification systems, we introduce AletheExt. Our extension enables Alethe to parse and generate proof formats from both COq and IsaFor, acting as an intermediate layer that simplifies the integration of Alethe's capabilities into these environments. We demonstrate the practicality of our approach by successfully extending COq automation to handle problems involving the COdo one-time pad and the advanced ChaCa-8 stream cipher, as well as enabling model checking within IsaFor for both the COdo one-time pad and the AAD-restricted ISO-8601 date formatting algorithm (using the IsofPc solver). In high-performance distributed environments, asynchronous data is frequently and accidentally submitted in non-constrained gradients due to diverse local computing speeds, network conditions, and heterogeneous client schedules. While prior research largely overlooked this phenomenon, we investigate its impact in the context of federated learning (FL) with unconstrained gradient updates. We introduce a novel buffered FL framework designed to manage asynchronous, unconstrained data. Our approach introduces the concepts of buffered mixing coefficient and effective batch size to theoretical analysis, proving that the algorithm converges linearly to the optimal solution under non-convex objectives within a number of rounds polynomial in precision's inverse. Empirical results from extensive tests on real-world infrastructures validate the framework's efficiency and flexibility, demonstrating superior FL performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Deep learning-driven automatic speech recognition (ASR) has seen significant advancements in transcription accuracy, yet a persistent challenge remains the scarcity of large, well-annotated datasets for specific target languages, dialects, or acoustic environments. To mitigate this limitation, we present a two-pronged strategy: first, we train acoustic models using diverse rough data sources—including unlabeled corpora and self-generated pseudo-labeled transcripts—and second, we deploy these models for cross-language transcription across various scenarios. Evaluation across three datasets confirms that incorporating rough data substantially boosts ASR performance relative to baseline acoustic models trained solely on clean labeled data. Furthermore, our cross-language transcription findings demonstrate successful generalization when testing languages distinct from the training languages.

Visualizing proximity-preserving representations of graph nodes, such as node2vec embeddings, enables their use in proximity-based machine learning models like neural networks for tasks such as node classification. Although various structural role-based methods exist for classifying nodes within graphs, there is currently no evaluation framework for graph representations intended for these specific proximity and role-based machine learning objectives. This paper introduces "Twitch Players," a comprehensive dataset designed to evaluate these models using both neural approaches and traditional techniques for related tasks. It applies neural classifiers to determine the Twitch streams of nodes represented by their Twitch2vec embeddings, achieving an 84.3% accuracy rate on the model's testing nodes. Additionally, the framework assesses traditional neural methods for Twitch2vec prediction tasks, yielding a accuracy rate of 84.3% on the dataset's testing nodes. This approach establishes a method for evaluating structural role-based graph representations for predictive tasks. Using this "Twitch Players" dataset, the study offers a comparative analysis of various Twitch2vec models, identifying the most suitable models for these specific role-based objectives.

The nature of the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance remains debated, specifically whether the $f_X(1500)$ represents a distinct state or a misidentified $D^*(1450)$ in $B\to \pi KK$ decays. This study utilizes $B\to \pi KK$ data collected by the Belle II experiment at the Belle Peak collider to analyze three channels: $B^0\to J/\psi K^+K^-$. By employing an updated amplitude analysis of $B^0\to J/\psi K^+K^+$ and $B^0\to J/\psi K^+K^+$, we determine the existence probability of the $f_X(1550)$ in $B\to \pi KK$ decays. We examine the dark sector in a low effective-dimensional regime, specifically within the framework of dark matter models where a significant portion consists of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs). In effective dimensions $d_{\text{eff}} < 3$, gravitational interactions become long-ranged and significantly stronger, altering the dynamical behavior of dark matter. We investigate whether such effects can account for the observed abundance of PBHs by analyzing whether small-seed PBHs accrete baryonic fuel and merge with other black holes in this environment. Unlike standard cosmological scenarios, merging PBHs in $d_{\text{eff}} < 3$ emit gravitational waves at frequencies within the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) observable range. Consequently, any remaining PBH population would generate detectable stochastic backgrounds. We further explore the intersection of these concepts with recent ideas regarding the Dark Matter fraction of PBHs ($f_{\rm PBH}$) and constraints derived from the Swampland Program.

This paper introduces a bidirectional force control method for series elastic actuators (SEAs) that leverages a force transmission observer to significantly improve precision. Observing that high-compliance mechanical transmissions introduce nonlinear force distortions difficult for standard observers to compensate, the authors propose a novel, highly robust estimation approach validated through simulations. Results demonstrate that with this strong transmission force observer integrated force control achieves optimal performance in both pressing and retrieval operations, achieving a 90% enhancement over current primary SEAs.

We examine the mechanics of brittle rafts adhering to a substrate through a framework of differential geometry, focusing on how fractures develop and alter the system's mechanical behavior. By analyzing both a uniform raft and one composed of segments with differing thermal expansion coefficients, we track fracture events from nucleation to propagation. We establish that expansion-driven compression is the primary cause of fracturing, while the resulting relief of compressive stresses induces contraction that triggers further fracturing during cooling. Specifically, the level of internal stress and the resulting strain energy density depends on the level of patterning, with maximum energy occurring at interfaces between adjacent rafts. Consequently, the energy stored during thermal cycling serves as a determining factor for the minimum size or contrast required in thermal expansion to avert internal failure. We also detail a mechanism by which the contractile forces of a cooling raft can forcibly break adhesion at the level of the substrate, leading to additional, complex failure modes. Our analysis includes a thermodynamic model for thermal stress propagation that parallels approaches used to understand rippling in monolayers, predicting that significant energy accumulates when a raft adheres to a patterned substrate with non-uniform thermal expansion properties.

This paper examines the relationship between inequity arising from chance variations in the allocation of income opportunities and the efficiency impacts depicted by income reallocation models. The mechanics of microorganisms are intimately linked to various biological and biotechnological processes. This study introduces a novel co-evolutionary approach to apply game theory within the context of population-level dynamics. The primary goal of federated learning is to train a shared model across multiple devices while maintaining local data privacy. The current state of Venus's atmosphere, characterized by extreme density and high surface temperatures, is widely viewed as the outcome of an irreversible runaway greenhouse effect. Initially, Earth-like surface conditions allowed solar radiation to reach the planetary core; however, subsequent increases in greenhouse gas concentrations triggered a positive feedback loop that escalated global warmth, drove the precipitation and dissolution of silicate minerals, released further greenhouse gases, and ultimately desiccated the planet's surface through prolonged insulating effects. Recent research, however, indicates that the loss of surface water may have stemmed directly from the degradation of the hydroxyl (OH) radical—a critical component in stratospheric photochemistry—caused by intensified ultraviolet fluxes and heightened concentrations of molecular hydrogen (H₂) and carbon monoxide (CO). This degradation likely occurred when Venus crossed a "tipping point," leading to the permanent transition into its present harsh state.

The nonlinear extension of the intensity-based self-exciting model (Hawkes process) involves mapping a historical trajectory to its corresponding generation times within the framework of hidden Markov models. Due to the prohibitively large computational demands required to handle the resulting state space dimensionality, standard inference approaches become unfeasible. We address this gap by developing a fully Bayesian inference framework designed to estimate a nonlinear multiawkes hidden task, specifically assuming an integer-order multiawkes structure (where $d$ denotes the number of streams). At its core lies a custom-built, low-dimensional, partially collapsed pseudo-marginal Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA). This algorithm streamlines posterior exploration by collapsing the integrals associated with the parameters of arrival intensities, incorporates stochastic gradient techniques for efficient optimization within stochastic perturbations, and targets the stochastic component of the posterior distribution. Furthermore, we introduce a novel, explicit stochastic perturbation term derived from the explicit form of the non-linear solution, ensuring efficient convergence during the posterior exploration phase. Numerical experiments and a real-world case study confirm the model's validity, demonstrating that these proposed methods successfully achieve consistent parameter estimation and outperform existing approaches in both speed and accuracy.

Driven by advancements in chirped pulse amplification, high-intensity laser technology has achieved unprecedented levels of power, allowing researchers to study nonlinear quantum phenomena and tailor material behavior. A critical factor in this evolution is the precise control of pulse polarization. Stacking numerous optical components to reach petawatt levels introduces nonlinear birefringence within the amplification chain, resulting in complex polarization states that are difficult to characterize and counteract. This paper presents a theoretical framework demonstrating that interacting petawatt pulses propagating through a pre-magnetized plasma can simultaneously amplify and simultaneously alter the polarization of counter-pumping beams concurrently. Unlike traditional methods relying on carefully tuned transverse magnetic fields, this approach utilizes the nonlinear magneto-optical effects inherent to the plasma to achieve the desired outcome. Specifically, by launching two counter-pumping, similarly intense pulses into a plasma with opposite longitudinal target magnetic field orientations, the interaction generates cross-polarized reflected components at specific conditions. This method offers a promising pathway for future petawatt laser facilities to ensure polarization purity.

We present optical/near-infrared (0.4–2.0 $\mu$m) observations of SN 2020jfo, a Type II-P supernova located 20.6 Mpc away. We propose a novel design for multiplexing multiple lobster-eye lenses (LELs) to create an alternative to the traditional single-unit approach. This architecture retains the instrument's inherent capability for direct hard X-ray timing while expanding the effective field of view (FOV). Suitable for observing phenomena such as gamma-ray burst afterglows, wide-FOV X-ray sky monitoring would also enable the detection and timing of cosmic events currently inferred only by multi-messenger signals, for example, astrophysical gravitational waves. The fundamental principles, performance characteristics, and feasible applications of this broadened FOV system is that we detail here through both theoretical analysis and ray-tracing simulations specific to our proposed configuration. Our results project a feasible FOV expansion up to roughly 10 degrees radius, spanning a spectral range from 2 to 30 keV, with spatial resolutions varying between 2.5 to 1 arcminutes.

For a class of fully nonlinear uniformly elliptic equations characterized by Lebesgue measurable data, we establish a version of boundary Liouville theory typically associated with constant coefficients. Specifically, we demonstrate that the statement holds when constant coefficients are substituted with those satisfying our specified conditions within a stadium-shaped domain. These coefficients are further required to be monotonic along specific streamline patterns. These patterns are defined as being comparable to, but distinct from, Stokes flows, gradients of harmonic functions, or stream functions. Notably, in square or rectangular domains, we show these general monotonic conditions reduce exactly to constant coefficients due to geometric constraints, whereas such an equivalence does not generally occur in domains of arbitrary geometry.

The influence of the large-scale cosmic velocity field on the evolution of dark matter halos remains an elusive research topic. Utilizing the extensive MaNGA dataset, we demonstrate that the velocity dispersion of dark matter halos exhibits a dependence on both the gravity-weighted velocity field at their location and the cross-correlation between this local field and the field at accretion peaks. Specifically, the simulation indicates that halos situated where both the gravity-weighted velocity field and its alignment with accretion peaks are strong tend to be more stripped and thus lighter for a given mass function. Conversely, halos forming in regions characterized by weak local velocity field values and poor alignment show reduced susceptibility to both outflows and stripping mechanisms. These findings provide a promising pathway for investigating how the spatially varying velocity field affects dark matter halo formation.

Music transcription involves converting audio signals into symbolic representations, such as MIDI or sheet music, serving as an indispensable step in music analysis workflows. Although automatic transcription systems have evolved significantly in recent years, robust performance remains elusive for complex instruments like the keyboard, largely due to the substantial labor required to annotate extensive training datasets. This study proposes an advanced score-observation model grounded in semi-supervised learning principles, designed to refine latent space learning by leveraging limited labeled data to guide the interpretation of vast amounts of unlabeled audio recordings. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that this learning framework surpasses state-oftheart deep learning approaches, achieving a F1 score of 0.699 on the challenging MEAD benchmark, an improvement of 10% over the previous best semi-supervised neural method (0.629). Furthermore, when tested against a naive fully-supervised neural baseline using massive amounts of annotated references, the proposed model delivers comparable performance (0.673) while achieving this result with far fewer labels.

This paper introduces a novel formulation for formulating the equilibrium structure of rotating stars that incorporates general relativity. By formulating the Einstein field equations using a 1+3 covariant decomposition relative to the vorticity vector and expressing them as a Poisson-like equation coupled with side relations for the energy-momentum tensor, structural determination reduces to solving this single equation alongside its associated boundary conditions. This method is particularly advantageous because it facilitates numerical solutions through standard shooting techniques. Furthermore, this approach streamlines the integration of various rotational patterns by expressing angular velocity as a function of specific invariants derived from the antisymmetric rotational Killing-Yano tensor. Utilizing this new formalism, we have generated rotation curves and equilibrium configurations consistent with our earlier work, which employed a highly effective 2+2 covariant decomposition. Results demonstrate that this proposed formulation yields results identical to those of the methodology developed in our study, thereby confirming its validity. Finally, the distinct benefits of this approach over conventional approaches, along with its broad applicability to rotating systems under diverse equation of states, have been clearly established.

Lack of adequately labeled training data is a significant obstacle to developing high-caliber automated systems for extracting information from visual documents. Existing approaches often depend on heuristics to preprocess unstructured inputs into structured formats prior to training, resulting in substantial engineering overhead, increased latency, and higher memory consumption. In this study, we introduce a straightforward, universal method for enhancing training data-labeling efficiency for extraction models operating on visual documents. By utilizing a lightweight fine-tuning process to convert sparse, high-quality labeled training data into an expansive corpus of "highly confident synthetic training data," our technique capitalizes on the propagable nature of model certainty. We specifically define "trusting-based self-annotation" as the reliable generation of these confident synthetic labels through extraction modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms current leading strategies, effectively delivering richly annotated training datasets with minimal latency and overhead.

The rate of gravitational waves (GWs) emitted by neutron star–black hole (NSBH) systems is projected to surpass that of binary black holes (BBHs) from gravitational-wave observatories such as LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA. However, the current ability to identify and classify these signals remains constrained. This research introduces a deep-learning framework designed to detect and classify GWs from inspiraling BBH, BH–NS, and NSBH systems. Utilizing the effective-one-body (EOB) formalism, we generated training data encompassing approximately 3.5 million parameter-space samples for these systems. We trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) via supervised learning to classify these signals in the time-frequency domain. The resulting models achieved an average confusion-matrix classification accuracy of 99.999% across the three system types. Furthermore, the trained CNN demonstrated the ability to distinguish individual signals from noise with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 5, successfully identifying BBH, BH–NS, and NSBH events at SNR levels between 5 and 10 with corresponding efficiencies of 94.999%, 94.999%, and 95%, respectively.

We introduce a framework designed to extract Social Determinants of Health (SOH)—external factors encompassing education, income, social connections, and living conditions that significantly impact an individual's physical and mental condition. While numerous natural language processing (NLP) tools exist for analyzing electronic health records (EHR), our approach specifically targets identifying SOH within those data. The core of this framework is a social determinant annotation (SDA) label applied to EHR structures, facilitating a versatile system for various annotation tasks. We evaluated the framework using two datasets: one containing de-identified, real-world EHR samples from the Mayo Clinic, and a simulated dataset populated with explicit SOH information. Results demonstrate high performance across both test environments, with the framework achieving an F1 score of 0.94 on the annotated clinical data.

This study analyzes the best movement strategy for relocating an active particle, known as a scallop, from one location to another within a viscous environment. Bestowing upon it a fixed sequence of shape changes (a kinematic program), we determine an advantageous temporal schedule for a scallop to traverse the shortest possible distance. While previous work addressed this for specific patterns, our approach is general; it applies to any shape change protocol and yields a travel-time scaling law of $T_{\min}\sim L^{2.5}$. Furthermore, we explore a scenario in an active fluid, termed a "nanosail," where the scallop interacts hydrodynamically with a fixed obstacle. We demonstrate that strategically timing the movement can enable a net displacement driven solely by interaction fluid flows, effectively overcoming the symmetry constraints that typically immobilize such particles at the low Reynolds number regime.

Utilizing a global urban mobility dataset, we examine how mobility patterns shifted between pre-pandemic baselines and post-pandemic recovery phases across 250 major cities. Our findings reveal that income-related disparities in mobility were amplified behaviorally during the crisis, even as most cities saw general mobilities return to pre-existing levels. However, the adaptive responses to the pandemic varied significantly by socioeconomic status: lower-income demographics exhibited stronger tendencies toward mobility mean-reversion, whereas higher-income groups maintained distinct deviations from pre-pandemic norms. These divergent adaptations highlight the fragility of lower-income mobility patterns during the health emergency and underscore the necessity for interventions tailored to specific socioeconomic contexts to mitigate unequal urban impacts.

Observations of young, high-mass stars reveal they undergo distinct growth phases marked by changes in their surrounding circumstellar disks. To investigate the causes of these phases, we developed a two-fluid, three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulation framework that tracks gas and dust separately. By applying this model to a specific star with a one solar mass infraction rate of $2.5 \times 10^{-5} M_{\odot}/\mathrm{yr}$, we analyzed how the forming central object generates powerful, collimated outflows and bipolar jets. These features trigger a pressure wave that propagates outward, clearing a low-density cavity through which jets and flows emerge. We demonstrate that this process results in a temporary reduction in the accretion rate onto the central star—an event-driven drop in accretion rate—an event-driven phenomenon known as an "accretion episode." This mechanism offers a plausible explanation for periodic variations observed in high-mass young stellar objects. Furthermore, we found that the model predicts a central star formation timescale of approximately 1 million years, consistent with current theoretical frameworks. Notably, when comparing our findings to a lower-resolution hydrodynamic model treating gas and dust as a single fluid, we observed that the inclusion of dust as a separate component significantly increases the mass of clumps formed within the infraction structure by a factor of 100.

This investigation explores the implications of scalar wedge quantum field theories characterized by sector-type local interactions and non-trivial, yet finite, conformal anomaly. We establish the existence of a theory satisfying the Poincaré wedge duality framework, confirming that its net of observables conforms to the KMS condition.

This study examines 5G base station radiation exposure levels across neighborhoods containing residential areas, schools, medical facilities, and residential complexes. Utilizing a newly developed, open-access, high-precision, three-dimensional model of a suburban zone in the United States, we reconstructed the exact positions of trees, power lines, and structures with high fidelity. By integrating measured emission data from multiple commercial vendors, this framework calculates radio wave exposure levels originating from nearby base stations. Numerical simulations were conducted to assess the impact of varying station counts and spatial distributions on radiation exposure in these different land-use scenarios. Results indicate that in residential settings, exposure levels for adults and children fluctuate between $0.0001$ and $0.001$ W/kg (averaging $0.0004$ W/kg) at typical home locations, and $0.0001$ to $0.001$ W/kg (averaging $0.0003$ W/kg) within yards. Conversely, exposure peaks are higher near educational and healthcare properties: average levels reach approximately $0.001$ W/kg near schools and $0.002$ W/kg near hospitals for both children and adults, with maximum values of $0.003$ W/kg for teenagers near schools and $0.004$ W/kg for children near hospitals.

By applying a hierarchy of transformations, we recast the two-dimensional, incompressible, and irrotational water wave problem with constant vorticity into a set of cubic equations. This formulation holds significant relevance for analyzing the stability of roll waves and constructing stochastic weak turbulence theories. Additionally, the derived hierarchy enables the derivation of the Dysthe formula, originally describing zero-vorticity waves, to apply scenarios involving vorticity. Specifically, this generalization allows for the derivation of the Dysthe-Liouville equation, which incorporates uniform non-zero vorticity as a boundary condition, within its extended form.

Developed initially for Puck robots, INM merges sonar, optical, and encoder information to deliver precise location estimates and collision avoidance commands. The rapid proliferation of news dissemination platforms on the internet has concurrently fueled a surge in fraudulent news, posing significant threats to public well-being and social stability. Effectively identifying and removing these news articles is now a critical challenge. Recently, deep learning-driven approaches have emerged as a popular solution; however, the necessity for vast amounts of labeled data keeps expanding, and the scarcity of such data continues to hinder progress. Furthermore, existing deep learning models often struggle to integrate domain-specific knowledge and fail to produce sufficiently interpretable outcomes. Addressing these issues, we introduced a novel framework for fraudulent news detection that leverages sequential automatic text summarization. Within this approach, our system generates concise narratives capturing the essence of entire news feeds and classifies them as either authentic or deceptive. Crucially, this method requires no data labeling beyond the final verdict on the summarized story, offering a significant advantage over frameworks dependent on heavily tagged datasets. Additionally, by focusing on content generation rather than complex content analysis, the model avoids the intricacies associated with maintaining data labels at the sentence level. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the FakeNews19 and TrueFalse datasets.

This work investigates security within non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), addressing the scenario where a NOMA decoder operates under an incorrect coding rate selection, termed "misdecoding." Finally, we evaluate the proposed scheme numerically, assessing its efficacy in terms of misdecoding probabilities and distoritions.

In the realm of fluid-structure interaction (FSI), identifying the most effective structural configurations within a specific design space is a critical objective. Design optimization for these systems is a complex endeavor, largely due to the high computational expense of solving the underlying FSI problem at each iteration. This study introduces a novel, iterative approach to the FSI Reduced Basis (FBT) technique, aiming to discover the optimal design by integrating reduced basis methods (RBM) with a sequential (partitioned) algorithm. Key attributes of this proposed FBT framework include a design-dependent reduced basis and a stable, convergent iterative procedure. A primary innovation lies in injecting passive structural modes into a sequential algorithm to enhance design convergence. The efficacy and precision of this method were validated through a benchmark case, demonstrating its robustness.

Current methods for mapping and navigating unfamiliar environments typically replace the original environment with a memory map that prioritizes a dense sample of its features. Although these approaches achieve good recognition accuracy, utilizing a highly dense feature set results in a large number of dimensions, which hinders efficient real-time layout classification. Furthermore, these strategies usually fail to incorporate the spatial relationships between individual features, treating the feature collection as unstructured and unordered. This paper proposes a hierarchical topological map (HiTMap) designed to navigate unknown spaces more effectively. It features a compact, organized system that leverages a multi-level spatial hierarchy to map the surrounding layout. Both the environment and the potential robot trajectories are approximated through this structured topological map, which significantly reduces the dimensions of the overall layout representation. These capabilities enable the robot to effectively classify its position within the environment and plan paths, even in areas not yet mapped. Beyond the immediate classification and planning modules, the structured nature of HiTMap offers distinct advantages for downstream perception and navigation tasks compared to standard point cloud alternatives.
